title: Request to Stop Fuel Weeping at Wing Tank Access Panels after Tank Entry
abstract: Operator reports fuel weeping from wing tank access panels within weeks of every tank entry, generating repeat defects, ramp fuel checks and occasional flight cancellations on its short-haul network.

sections.request: Every time we open a wing tank, whether for a boost pump, a probe or a scheduled internal inspection, we are back in the same panel within three or four weeks with fuel weeping at the edge. Our line stations wipe it, we watch it, and eventually we take the panel off again, clean everything down and reseal, and then it comes back. It is not dramatic but it is constant, it makes the aircraft look bad on the ramp, and twice in the last year we have had to cancel a first sector because the weep had turned into a visible drip overnight. We are not asking for a redesign of the wing. We want a panel and a seal arrangement that survives ten years of normal tank entries without weeping.
sections.background: Across our fleet we log around ninety tank entries a year and roughly one in three produces a weeping defect within the first month. Our own investigation points at the combination of the panel seal groove and the fastener torque sequence, because the weep is nearly always at the same two positions on the panel. We have tried extending the sealant cure time and we have tried a different sealant class, and neither has changed the rate. The MRO that does our heavy checks reports the same experience across three other operators of the type.
sections.expected_outcome: A wing tank access panel installation that can be opened and closed by a normal line or base maintenance team, using published torque values and a single sealant, and that does not weep within the first year after closure. A repeatable closure that does not depend on the individual mechanic would be worth more to us than a marginal weight saving.

type_data.business_justification: Around thirty repeat weeping defects a year, each consuming a night stop and a two-person crew, plus two cancellations in the last twelve months. The operator values the direct maintenance cost at 410 thousand euros a year and considers the reputational cost of visible fuel on the ramp to be higher still.
